opus-5.5.text:
Thank you, Xiaojun, it's a pleasure to be here.

That's a big question, and I'll answer it from my own angle, which is embodied intelligence. For me, intelligence is fundamentally about an agent achieving its goals in a complex, uncertain world. It isn't just answering questions or producing fluent text. It's the ability to perceive the environment, understand what's happening, make decisions, and then act, so that the world actually changes in the way you intended. Then you take in feedback and keep adjusting.

If you look at it through evolution, intelligence didn't start with language. It started with movement. Animals needed to find food, avoid danger, and manipulate objects, so they developed brains to coordinate perception and action. Language and abstract reasoning came very late, sitting on top of this huge foundation of sensorimotor ability. That's Moravec's paradox: what feels hard to us, like chess or math, turned out to be relatively easy for machines, and what feels effortless, like picking up a cup or folding clothes, is extremely hard for robots.

So large language models are remarkable. They've compressed an enormous amount of human knowledge, and in a sense they've captured part of the "mind." But they mostly live in the world of symbols. They haven't truly grounded that knowledge in physical interaction: forces, contact, friction, what happens when you push something. I think a complete intelligence has to close that loop between perception, cognition, and action in the physical world.

So my short answer is that intelligence is the capability to generalize: to face situations you've never seen before and still act effectively toward a goal. Generalization is the core. And for us working on robots, the real test is whether a machine can enter an unfamiliar home or factory and get things done, not just perform well on the data it was trained on. That's the gap we're trying to close.

r001.rationale: The response describes intelligence as perceiving a situation and acting effectively toward a goal, including adapting to unfamiliar situations—an equivalent formulation of responding appropriately to the situation encountered.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. That's a question I've turned over for years, and my answer keeps getting simpler rather than more complicated.

I think the essence of intelligence is the ability to form a model of the world and then act on it in ways that compress the distance between what you want and what is. It's not memory, it's not raw computation, and it's not even knowledge. Knowledge is a byproduct. The core is a loop: perceive, predict, act, and then update when the prediction turns out wrong. The quality of intelligence is really the quality of that update step.

When I look at this from a robotics perspective, I find it clarifying, because a robot can't fake it. A language model can produce a fluent paragraph about pouring water into a cup without ever having touched water. A robot has to actually pour, and the physics gives it a grade immediately. So embodiment forces you to confront what intelligence really has to do, which is deal with a world that is continuous, partially observed, and indifferent to your beliefs about it.

There's a second piece I'd add, which is generalization. A system that handles a thousand memorized situations isn't intelligent; it's a lookup table. Intelligence shows up precisely at the edge, when the situation is new and you still do something sensible. Humans are remarkable at this. A child who has never seen a particular chair knows how to sit in it. That transfer, from the structure of past experience to a novel instance, is what we're really chasing.

And a third piece, which I think gets underweighted: intelligence is fundamentally about efficiency. Evolution did not produce brains that consume unlimited data. A person learns to drive in about twenty hours. Our current systems need something closer to millions of simulated hours. So when someone shows me a model that performs well, my first question is not how well, but at what cost in data and experience. The gap between those two numbers tells you how much of the essence we've actually captured and how much we've substituted with scale.

So if I had to compress it: intelligence is efficient, generalizable modeling of the world in service of action. Everything else, language, reasoning, creativity, I see as instruments that serve that loop, rather than the thing itself.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes intelligence as modeling the world and acting on that model, including doing something sensible in new situations, which conveys responding appropriately to the situation encountered.

astra-6.text:
I think the essence of intelligence is the ability to learn from experience and act effectively in a changing world. It’s more than knowing facts or producing an answer. You need to recognize what matters, anticipate the consequences of your actions, and revise your understanding when reality surprises you.

Imagine encountering a situation you’ve never seen before. Can you draw on what you already know, identify what you don’t know, and figure out what to try next? That ability to adapt is central to intelligence.

And intelligence doesn’t necessarily mean getting everything right the first time. Sometimes the most intelligent thing you can do is ask a good question, run a small experiment, or admit that your current explanation is wrong. So I see intelligence as an ongoing interaction between learning, reasoning, and action.

r001.rationale: It describes intelligence as learning and acting effectively in a changing world, and says adaptation to an unfamiliar situation is central.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the essence of intelligence is the ability to build an understanding of the world and use it to act in unfamiliar situations. It’s more than remembering facts or recognizing patterns. You need to work out what matters, anticipate what might happen, and revise your understanding when reality surprises you.

For example, if you encounter a problem you’ve never seen before, can you draw on past experience without being trapped by it? Can you explore, learn from feedback, and find a useful solution? That ability to adapt is central to intelligence.

And I would distinguish intelligence from knowledge. Knowledge is what you’ve accumulated; intelligence is what allows you to keep learning and make use of what you know.

r001.rationale: The response describes using an understanding of the world to act in unfamiliar situations, adapt to feedback, and find a useful solution, conveying the ability to respond suitably to a situation.
